newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Fischler warns against new EU grain mountains.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Fischler warns against new EU grain mountains.

text.p: More reforms are needed to curb an alarming increase in European Union grain output and prevent grain mountains reappearing, EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Wednesday.
EU grain farmers, encouraged by high prices and a relaxation of planting restrictions, produced a record 202 million tonnes in 1996, 27 million tonnes more than in 1995.
Fischler said grain output could surge a further 10 percent in 1997 after the proportion of land that farmers must take out of production to qualify for EU subsidies was halved to five percent.
"(Lower set-aside) coupled with the annual increase in average yields is alarming," Fischler told a news conference to present farm price proposals for the year starting July 1.
Public grain stocks, which peaked at 33 million tonnes in 1993 before radical reforms in 1992 sent them plunging to under three million tonnes last year, are set to soar this season.

Although the EU's executive proposed mainly unchanged farm support prices over the coming year, it reiterated a call for a 1.4-billion-Ecu ($1.6 billion) cut in direct aid payments to cereals and oilseed farmers.
The payments were agreed under the 1992 price- and production-cutting reforms to compensate farmers for revenue losses. But since then market prices have soared.
Farm incomes among the EU's eight million farmers rose by 4.8 percent in 1996. Following substantial rises since 1993, they are now at their highest level for more than 20 years.

The Commission first proposed a cut in cereals payments last summer to help fund emergency aid for beef farmers devastated by a fall in demand after scared shoppers switched to lamb and pork because of a health scare over mad cow disease.
EU farm ministers threw out the proposal in October and instead found funds by delaying some oilseed aid payments.

They are again set to react angrily after German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert on Wednesday fired the first broadside. "This (proposal) undermines the confidence of farmers and credibility of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)," he said in a statement.
German and EU farmers needed these payments to cover their costs and stay on the land, he added.
Fischler stressed that further reforms would be needed to prepare for the next round of world farm trade talks starting in 1999 and the EU's expansion eastwards early next century.
The impact of 1992 price-cutting reforms will also have bottomed out by the end of the decade, he noted.

To help prepare for further reforms, the Commission is due to complete by the end of March a detailed analysis of domestic and international cereals, dairy and beef production and market trends over the next five to 10 years.
For the key grain sector, a choice would have to be made: either cereals set-aside rates were increased to curb production, or export subsidies were removed and the EU exported freely, he said.
Otherwise the EU would in a couple of years run into GATT (General Agrement on Traiffs and Trade) limits on subsidised grain exports, he said.
"A policy such as the CAP (Common Agricultural Policy) ...cannot stand still," he said, adding: "My objective is to ensure that new grain mountains are not formed."
